questions.prompt: State the two closure properties required for a real vector space.
questions.answer: A real vector space must be closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication. Closure under addition means that if u and v are in the space, then u + v is also in the space. Closure under scalar multiplication means that if c is a real scalar and v is in the space, then cv is also in the space.

questions.prompt: Explain why the set of all real polynomials P is a real vector space under usual addition and scalar multiplication.
questions.answer: The sum of two real polynomials is again a real polynomial, so addition closure holds. A real scalar times a real polynomial is again a real polynomial, so scalar closure holds. The zero polynomial acts as the additive identity, and additive inverses are obtained by negating coefficients. The usual algebraic laws come from real-number arithmetic. Therefore P is a real vector space.

questions.prompt: Decide whether the set of polynomials of degree exactly 2 is a vector space.
questions.answer: It is not a vector space. For example, \(p(x)=x^2\) and \(q(x)=-x^2\) both have degree exactly 2, but \(p(x)+q(x)=0\). The zero polynomial does not have degree exactly 2. Addition closure fails, so the set is not a vector space.

questions.prompt: Explain why the set \(M_{2,2}(\mathbb R)\) of all \(2\times 2\) real matrices is a real vector space.
questions.answer: Adding two \(2\times 2\) real matrices produces another \(2\times 2\) real matrix, and multiplying a \(2\times 2\) real matrix by a real scalar produces another \(2\times 2\) real matrix. The zero matrix is the additive identity, and each matrix has an additive inverse obtained by negating all entries. The vector-space laws hold entry by entry from real arithmetic. Therefore \(M_{2,2}(\mathbb R)\) is a real vector space.

questions.prompt: Decide whether the set of positive real numbers is a vector space under usual addition and scalar multiplication.
questions.answer: It is not a vector space. The zero vector would have to be 0, but 0 is not positive. Also scalar closure fails: 1 is positive, but (-1)*1 = -1 is not positive. Therefore the positive real numbers are not a real vector space under usual operations.

questions.prompt: Show that the set C\((0,1)\) of continuous real-valued functions on \((0,1)\) is a real vector space.
questions.answer: The sum of two continuous functions on \((0,1)\) is continuous, so addition closure holds. A real scalar multiple of a continuous function is continuous, so scalar closure holds. The zero function is continuous and acts as the additive identity. Additive inverses are continuous because -f is continuous whenever f is continuous. The usual function operations satisfy the vector-space laws pointwise. Therefore C\((0,1)\) is a real vector space.

questions.prompt: Decide whether the set of functions f with \(f(0)\) = 1 is a vector space under usual function operations.
questions.answer: It is not a vector space. A vector space must contain the zero function, but the zero function has value 0 at \(x=0\), not 1. Also, if \(f(0)\) = 1, then 2f has value 2 at \(x=0\), so scalar closure fails. Therefore the set is not a vector space.

questions.prompt: Give the zero vector in the vector space \(P_3\) of polynomials of degree at most 3.
questions.answer: The zero vector is the additive identity for polynomial addition. In \(P_3\), this is the zero polynomial 0, whose value is 0 for every input. It has coefficients all equal to zero, so \(p(x)=0\).

questions.prompt: Find the additive inverse of \(p(x)=2-3x+x^2\) in \(P_2\).
questions.answer: The additive inverse is the polynomial q(x) such that p(x) + q(x) = 0. Negate every coefficient of p. Therefore q(x) = -2 + 3x - \(x^2\). Indeed, (2 - 3x + \(x^2\)) + (-2 + 3x - \(x^2\)) = 0.

questions.prompt: A learner says vector spaces must contain arrows or coordinate tuples. Diagnose the error.
questions.answer: A vector space is defined by operations and axioms, not by what its elements look like. Polynomials, matrices, and functions can be vectors if they can be added and scaled in a way that satisfies the vector-space laws. Coordinate tuples are only one important example. The learner is confusing geometric vectors with the more general algebraic idea of vectors.
